title: What Would Europe Do in a Taiwan Crisis?
text:
What Would Europe Do in a Taiwan Crisis?

The Diplomat

Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty Images

The following is an excerpt from an op-ed published in The Diplomat on October 6, 2026, written by Simona Grano, Senior Fellow on Taiwan at ASPI's Center for China Analysis.Imagine that, one morning, Chinese coast guard vessels begin stopping commercial ships approaching Taiwan. Beijing offers the official explanation that the operation is necessary to enforce customs regulations and maritime safety and makes clear that it does not consider this a blockade, let alone an act of war. Taipei clearly sees things differently and calls it an attempt to blockade the island. Washington agrees with Taipei.Europe, however, is less certain, with some governments demanding that China stop its actions while others start calling for restraint and dialogue. Officials begin debating whether the operation constitutes an armed attack, what international law permits, and whether sanctions against China would be justified. Meanwhile the effects on global trade start to be felt as insurers raise premiums, shipping companies start to reroute vessels, and financial markets react nervously.At that point, Washington steps up and asks its European allies to impose economic costs on Beijing. The answer from Europe could very likely be an attempt to win more time to determine what is happening. That delay could incidentally be precisely what Beijing is aiming to achieve: deliberate ambiguity, namely the systematic creation of legal and political uncertainty designed to make an adversary hesitate over how to respond.Read the full op-ed here.
